meta.title: Who really said "Each person must live their life as a model for others"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rosa Parks is universally credited with this line, but no book, speech, or interview has ever been pinned to it — the popular “Quiet Strength” source is unconfirmed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Each person must live their life as a model for others'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Rosa Parks everywhere, sourced nowhere: the line is absent from Wikiquote and no primary text has been located for it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Universally credited to Rosa Parks and consistent with her emphasis on personal moral example — but no primary source (book, page, speech, interview, or letter) has been located that contains this exact wording. The frequently repeated claim that it comes from her 1994 reflection book Quiet Strength circulates without any page reference and could not be confirmed, so the exact line remains attributed rather than documented.

source.heading: The sourcing problem
source.excerpt: Each person must live their life as a model for others.
trail: Attributed to Rosa Parks across quote databases such as Goodreads and BrainyQuote — none of which cite a book, speech, or date.
It is absent from Wikiquote’s Rosa Parks page, which lists her sourced and attributed quotations but not this one.
A 2013 blog post that helped popularize it openly sourced the line to Twitter and BrainyQuote, not to any Parks work.
Her 1994 book Quiet Strength is often named as the source, but no page citation is ever given and the wording could not be confirmed in its text.
source.excerptNote: The line is almost always reproduced bare, with no surrounding passage, speech occasion, or page — a hallmark of a quotation that entered circulation through aggregators rather than a source text.
source.rightsNote: The origin of this exact wording is undetermined, so no rights status can be asserted. If it were genuinely drawn from Quiet Strength (Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 1994), it would be in copyright (Rosa Parks estate / Zondervan); but because that source is unconfirmed and no other primary text has been found, the status is honestly uncertain — and no public-domain claim is made.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: Who was Rosa Parks?
author.metaLine: 1913–2005 · American civil rights activist, "Mother of the Civil Rights Movement"
author.bio: Rosa Louise McCauley Parks (1913–2005) was an American activist whose refusal to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, on December 1, 1955, sparked the Montgomery bus boycott and became a catalyst of the modern civil rights movement. Often called the “Mother of the Civil Rights Movement,” she remained active for decades and co-founded the Rosa and Raymond Parks Institute for Self Development. Her books Rosa Parks: My Story (1992) and Quiet Strength (1994) recount her life and faith.

misattribution.heading: A sourceless attribution
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the words belonging to someone else — it is a case of a warm, aphoristic line pinned to a beloved name with no source ever attached. That is exactly how fabricated or heavily paraphrased “quotes” take root online.

items.why: Many sites assert the line comes from Parks’ book Quiet Strength, but none supply a page number and the wording could not be located in the book’s record. The “source” appears to be a later back-fill, not a citation.
The earliest readily traceable circulation runs through databases and Twitter — a 2013 post that reproduced it credited “Twitter” and BrainyQuote as its verification, not any Parks speech or writing.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment fits Rosa Parks, but the sentence has no documented home in her speeches or books — and it is telling that Wikiquote does not list it at all.

context.heading: Why the caution
lead: Rosa Parks genuinely did speak in terms of personal example — her whole public meaning is that one quiet act of principle can model courage for millions. That is precisely why a line like this attaches to her so easily and feels right, which is also why it deserves scrutiny rather than a reflexive stamp of approval.
On a verified-provenance site the honest verdict is: credibly hers in spirit, but undocumented in wording. Until a specific page, speech, or interview surfaces, “attributed” is the accurate label.
context.pull: Fits her spirit; found in none of her documented words.
